submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole is a word-level detector for the concrete hardware-and-materials vocabulary of technical prose: it peaks on the nouns for casings, fittings and mechanical parts (casing, enclosure, housing, shell, chassis, cabinet, seal, bearing, screw, lock, spring, frame, filter, tank, pump, motor, generator, door) and on their material words (metal, plastic, aluminum, concrete), reaching several times its 0.34 scan maximum on that word alone - 'The equipment was sealed in a metal casing' 5.9 on 'casing', 'The sensor is enclosed in a plastic housing' 5.6 on 'housing' - while the same frame with the everyday near-synonym leaves the word empty ('We replaced the casing' 4.75 vs 'We replaced the container' 0.00; 'We replaced the motor' 0.26 vs 'We replaced the engine' 0.00). It reads the word rather than preparing the next one (the Jacobian and logit lenses share no token, kurtosis 2.9, and zeroing the pole moves the next-token distribution by KL 3e-5 with no concentrated target), and the words themselves stay at zero for everyday objects, people, animals, food and abstract nouns (car, table, cup, book, dog, cat, bread, idea, policy) and for the common mechanism/material words engine, machine, valve, pipe, gear, wheel, steel, wood and glass. Caveat for labelling: the scan's corpus is 9-21-token sentences and never contained this vocabulary, so its 0.34 maximum is the pole's shallow SwiGLU double-negative background, which ordinary prose also reaches (0.05-0.3, often above the scan-scale active threshold); the reliable signature is a large peak on the hardware/material word itself, not any single token of a plain sentence.

adversarial_test_results.prompt: At six in the morning the bus left the depot with only nine passengers aboard. The driver, a quiet man named Oren, kept both hands on the wheel as the city streets gave way to fields of dry grass. For an hour nobody spoke. A woman in the third row peeled an orange and passed the sections to the child beside her, and the child ate them slowly, one at a time, watching the fence posts slide past. By eight the sun had climbed above the treeline and the inside of the bus grew warm and sleepy. Oren turned on the radio, found a station playing old songs, and left it there. The road climbed through low hills where sheep stood in the shade of scattered oaks. At a crossroads a sign pointed toward a town none of the passengers had heard of, and the bus did not turn. Somewhere past the second hour the engine began to make a small, uneven sound, a tick that came and went with the slope of the road. Oren frowned and watched the gauges. He pulled into a service yard outside a village and asked the woman there to take a look. She listened to the tick, opened the front panel, and walked around to the front of the bus. She knelt, wiped the dust from the hub with a rag, and rocked the wheel with both hands. 'Front wheel bearing,' she said at last. 'It is running dry. I can pack it with grease and you will make your next town, but it wants replacing before the week is out.' Oren thanked her, paid in cash, and stood in the yard while she worked. The morning had turned bright and the hills looked closer than they had from the road. When she was done the tick was gone. The passengers climbed back aboard, and the bus rolled on through a country of stone walls and small brown rivers. A boy near the back counted the bridges out loud, losing track somewhere after seven and starting again. Nobody minded. At a small station a woman with a heavy suitcase got off, and an old man with a bicycle got on, and the bus started again before either of them had found a seat. The road bent north and followed a river for a while, and on the far bank a man was teaching a dog to swim. The dog paddled in circles and refused to come out, and the man laughed and waded in after it. In the seat ahead of her the woman with the orange had fallen asleep with her hat over her face. The boy had stopped counting and was drawing bridges in the dust on the window. They stopped once more, at a bakery beside a roundabout, and the driver bought a paper bag of rolls to share. The afternoon light was gold by the time the first houses of the next town appeared, and the bus slowed, and the people gathered their bags.
